pairs.rationale: Both ascribe prophetic communication to God. Hebrews says God spoke long ago to the fathers in prophets in many portions and ways; Peter says human beings spoke from God, borne along by the Holy Spirit rather than human will. The timing, means and Spirit detail are not treated as identical wording.

Both describe creative agency through the figure being discussed. Hebrews says God made the ages through the Son whom He appointed heir; Colossians says all things were created in, through and for Him. Ages is not silently replaced with all things, and the distinct in/through/for and heir clauses remain.

Upholding all things by the word of His power corresponds to all things holding together in Him. Colossians also says He is before all things; Hebrews adds radiance, imprint, purification and enthronement. The sustaining descriptions are compared without importing every additional claim into the other unit.

Both connect exalted status with the name bestowed or inherited. Philippians says God highly exalted Him and gave the name above every name; Hebrews compares His inherited name with theirs in describing superiority to angels. The granted/inherited and every-name/angels formulations remain distinct, without supplying an unprinted name here.

The first son-and-today-begotten saying closely matches the Lord's decree in Psalm2:7. The Psalm's appointed-king context says son in its own printed case and pronouns; Hebrews applies the saying in the Son-versus-angels question. No particular begetting date or an explicit Jesus name is added to the Psalm.

The Father-to-him and Son-to-Me promise closely corresponds to Samuel's father/son promise in a house-and-throne context. Samuel continues with correction if wrongdoing comes; Hebrews quotes the shorter relationship promise in its angel contrast. That unquoted wrongdoing clause is not assigned to Jesus.

The call for all His angels to bow down in the Psalm corresponds to all God's angels worshiping the firstborn here. The Psalm also rebukes carved-image worship; Hebrews frames the saying through bringing the firstborn into the inhabited world. That setting and again wording are not dated or added to the Psalm.

The makes-His-angels and ministers-as-fire formula closely corresponds to the Psalm. The supplied Psalm says angels winds and ministers a burning fire; Hebrews says angels spirits and ministers a flame of fire. Winds and spirits remain as actually translated rather than silently normalized.

The throne address to God, enduring-age language and upright royal rod or scepter correspond closely to Psalm44:7. Hebrews explicitly introduces the address as concerning the Son and says scepter where the Psalm says rod. Their age-of-age and age-upon-age wording and original pronouns remain intact.

The loved-righteousness/hated-lawlessness sequence and God-your-God anointing with oil of exultation beyond companions closely match Psalm44:8. Hebrews continues its quoted address concerning the Son; the Psalm's accompanying royal garment and palace setting is not inserted into the unit.

The beginning, Lord, earth's foundation and heavens-as-handworks statement closely corresponds to Psalm101:26. Hebrews introduces it within its Son-and-angels argument; the Psalm's surrounding plea about the speaker's days is not added to that quoted creation statement.

The perishing creation, remaining addressee and garment-aging contrast closely match Psalm101:27. That Psalm unit also continues into changing the cloak; Hebrews' unit ends at growing old and continues its quotation in1:12. The original unit boundaries are retained.

The cloak/garment change and unchanged addressee with unfailing years correspond to Psalm101:27–28. Hebrews says roll them up and adds like a garment before changed; the Psalm says change them like a cloak. The close quotation retains that actual roll/change difference.

The sit-at-My-right-hand and enemies-as-footstool saying closely matches Psalm109:1. The Psalm introduces the Lord speaking to my lord; Hebrews asks to which angel such speech was ever addressed. That argumentative application is not represented as a question already printed in the Psalm.

The Psalm gives a specific angel-service description: God commands His angels to guard the addressed person and lift him on their hands. Hebrews describes ministering spirits sent for the sake of salvation's heirs. Guarding in one's ways and the broader service-for-heirs statement remain distinct, without turning physical protection into an identical full salvation claim.

The later neglect-and-escape question identifies the great salvation message first spoken through the Lord and confirmed by hearers. It supplies the immediate message-and-consequence context for paying greater attention to what was heard. This is the argument's internal hearing/neglect connection, without turning drifting into a narrated physical journey.

Both speak of communication through angels and connect it with transgressions. Galatians names the law ordained through angels by a mediator and its until-the-seed purpose; Hebrews names the word becoming firm and just recompense for disobedience. The mediation, purpose and punishment clauses are retained as distinct descriptions.

Both describe reception from earlier witnesses. Hebrews says salvation was first spoken through the Lord and confirmed by those who heard; Luke says those who were eyewitnesses and servants of the word from the beginning handed them down to us. The hearing/eyewitness and confirmed/handed-down forms do not identify the groups or authors as one or specify one identical transmission process.

Both connect mighty deeds or acts of power with distributions associated with the Spirit and will. Hebrews names God bearing witness through signs, mighty deeds and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to His own will; Corinthians names the one Spirit working and distributing to each as He wills. Their witness and communal-gift purposes and different grammatical acting roles remain explicit.

The later subjection quotation and Jesus statement develop this world-to-come and angels contrast. They say all is subjected beneath his feet while not yet seen as subjected, and then explicitly present Jesus crowned through death. This is internal exposition, preserving both the negative about angels and the not-yet qualification.

The human-being/son-of-man question about divine remembrance closely corresponds to Psalm8:5. Hebrews says carest where the supplied Psalm says visitest; the preceding heavens context and the quotation's human reference are preserved without changing the whole target into one identical English sentence.

The lower-than-angels and glory-and-honor crowning clauses closely match Psalm8:6. The Psalm continues in the next unit into appointment over handworks; that additional clause is absent from the short original Hebrews2:7 and is not inserted into its body.

The subjecting-all-things-beneath-his-feet clause closely corresponds to Psalm8:7. The Psalm also names appointment over God's handworks; Hebrews follows its shorter quotation with an all-inclusive explanation and a not-yet-seen qualification. Those additional source and target statements remain distinct.

Both connect death and humiliation with subsequent honor or exaltation. Philippians names obedience to cross-death followed by God's high exaltation and granted name; Hebrews names Jesus' lower-than-angels position, suffering death, glory and honor, and death for everyone by God's grace. The stated reasons, images and beneficiaries are not made identical.

The later Son-through-suffering, perfected, source-of-salvation sequence repeats the suffering/perfection/salvation pattern here. It adds learning obedience and salvation for those obeying; this unit names the pioneer and many sons brought to glory. Pioneer and source and the different acting and receiving roles remain as printed, without an invented earlier moral failure.

John explicitly has Jesus call the disciples My brothers while naming My Father and your Father. That is a specific counterpart to not being ashamed to call the sanctified brothers here. Hebrews' all-from-one wording remains without assigning that unnamed one a further identity or making every surrounding kinship expression identical.

The name-to-brothers and assembly-praise saying closely corresponds to Psalm21:23. The Psalm says recount and sing hymns; Hebrews says announce and sing praise within the brothers argument. Those actual English forms and the Psalm's surrounding rescue-and-praise context are preserved.

The put-my-trust-in-Him clause closely matches Isaiah8:17. Isaiah's fuller utterance also waits for God who turned His face from Jacob's house; Hebrews uses the trust saying within its brothers-and-children argument. The shared I/Him wording does not by itself name every speaker or reproduce the full setting.

The I-and-the-children-God-gave-me clause directly corresponds to Isaiah8:18. Isaiah continues into signs and wonders in Israel's house and the Lord Sabaoth on Zion; Hebrews quotes the kinship statement without those additions. It does not identify the Isaiah children and the Hebrews community as the same historical individuals.

Both state a purpose of counteracting the devil. Hebrews names participation in blood and flesh and death to render the holder of death's power powerless; John names the Son of God manifested to undo the devil's works. The means, power-of-death and works language remain distinct.

Both relate slavery and fear to a changed saving relation. Hebrews specifies lifelong slavery through fear of death and release; Romans contrasts a spirit of slavery leading to fear with the Spirit of adoption. Death-fear, adoption and the distinct agents and descriptions are not simply made the same wording.

Both explicitly name Abraham's seed in relation to Christ's saving community. Galatians says those belonging to Christ are that seed and heirs of promise; Hebrews contrasts angels with the seed as the object of His taking hold. Takes hold is retained rather than expanded with unprinted nature-assumption wording.

Both connect the high priest with likeness to those He serves. The later unit names sympathy with weaknesses and testing as we are, yet without sin; this unit names being like His brothers, mercy and faithfulness, and propitiation for the people's sins. The testing, sinlessness and priestly-work clauses retain their own scope.

The later account joins a high priest tested as we are with approaching for mercy and timely help. It develops this connection between His own suffering when tested and ability to help the tested. Tested is preserved, and neither passage is made to state that He succumbed to sin.

Both name Jesus, high priest and confession. The later unit calls Him the Son of God who passed through the heavens and urges holding the confession; this unit addresses heavenly-call participants and also calls Jesus apostle. Heavenly calling is not replaced with the priest's own heaven-passing description.

The Moses-faithful-in-all-the-house formula closely corresponds to Numbers12:7. Numbers has God say My servant and My house; Hebrews compares Jesus' faithfulness to His appointer with Moses in His house. The pronouns and the Jesus comparison are not inserted into the Numbers unit.

The next house-and-builder statement develops the analogy behind greater honor for the builder than the house. It names every house's builder and God as builder of all; this unit applies the honor comparison to Jesus and Moses. The internal reasoning is preserved without identifying an unprinted physical building.

Both name God in relation to making or building all things. Acts names the world and everything in it and denies dwelling in handmade sanctuaries; Hebrews distinguishes each house's builder and God as builder of all. The creation and house analogy are related without making their sanctuary and honor arguments identical.

Moses faithful in all His house closely repeats Numbers12:7. The target calls him My servant, while Hebrews calls him an attendant and adds testimony concerning things to be spoken. The servant/attendant forms, pronouns and additional testimony clause retain their actual differences.

Both describe the believing community with a house or household image. Timothy explicitly calls God's household the Church of the living God and discusses conduct; Hebrews names Christ as Son over His house and says we are that house with a hold-fast condition. The conditional confidence/hope assertion and the Church description remain distinct.

The Today-if-you-hear-His-voice call corresponds to the end of Psalm94:7. Hebrews attributes the quotation to the Holy Spirit; the Psalm also names our God, pasture people and sheep of His hand. That attribution and the additional pastoral clauses are not silently written into each other's units.

The no-hardening, provocation and wilderness-testing-day wording closely matches Psalm94:8. Hebrews places the saying within its Spirit-attributed warning; the Psalm supplies the same admonition in its own worship-and-warning sequence. The original verse boundaries remain unchanged.

Both recall ancestors testing and seeing My works. Hebrews says fathers tested Me with a trial; the Psalm says ancestors tested, put to the proof. The actual subject, Me and trial/proof wording are preserved; the forty-years phrase is not moved into this source unit.

The generation's wandering or straying heart and not knowing My ways correspond closely to Psalm94:10. Hebrews begins for forty years completing the preceding saw-My-works clause, then says Therefore I was indignant with this generation; the Psalm places forty years with being vexed with that generation. The clause attachment, this/that and indignant/vexed differences remain intact.

The sworn exclusion from My rest corresponds directly to Psalm94:11. Hebrews says wrath and certainly not; the supplied Psalm says anger and shall not. The negative oath remains without replacing one unit's English emphasis with the other's.

Both warn of inner turning away from God. The actual Greek-based Deuteronomy29:17 asks about a mind turned aside from the Lord to serve other gods; Hebrews warns of an evil unbelieving heart turning from the living God. Mind/heart and idolatry/unbelief descriptions are not normalized, and the target is not misnumbered29:18.

Both direct mutual encouragement. Thessalonians adds building each other up and acknowledges the readers already doing so; Hebrews specifies each day during Today to prevent hardening by sin's deceit. The shared instruction retains those different purposes and qualifications.

Both attach continued firm trust to the described benefit. Hebrews names becoming Christ's partakers if the beginning of confidence is held firm to the end; Colossians names continuing in founded, steadfast faith without shifting from gospel hope in the presentation context. The conditional forms and different benefits remain without a further theory about unstated cases.

The repeated Today, hearing His voice and no-hardening-as-in-provocation saying corresponds to Psalm94:7–8. The selected full Psalm units also contain pasture/sheep and wilderness-day clauses not all repeated here. The shorter quotation is preserved without completing it with unprinted extra words.

Numbers reports all Israel grumbling against Moses and Aaron and wishing to have died in Egypt or the wilderness. That supplies concrete rebellion background for the question about those hearing and coming out of Egypt through Moses. Hebrews' was-it-not-all question and Numbers' report retain their actual forms, rather than rewriting the source as a not-all statement.

The bodies-falling and forty-year wilderness outcome has a concrete counterpart in Numbers' sentence upon counted adult grumblers. Numbers also distinguishes Caleb, Joshua and the children, and names the sons' forty years as herders; Hebrews asks about sinners whose bodies fell. Those age, exception and child distinctions remain visible rather than being silently erased.

The question interprets the earlier sworn no-entry-rest language, which directly corresponds to Psalm94:11. The Psalm gives the oath in anger; Hebrews identifies the disobedient as its subjects. That interpretive identification is not inserted into the Psalm's single unit.

Numbers explicitly gives the Lord's accusation that the people refuse to believe despite His signs. That is a specific unbelief counterpart to Hebrews' conclusion that they could not enter because of unbelief. The narrative charge and the entry conclusion remain distinct statements.
